subtopic 2not assigned (one subtopic chosen)

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
When two monochromatic lights of frequency, ν and ν2 are incident on a photoelectric metal, their stopping potential becomes Vs2 and Vs respectively. The threshold frequency for this metal is
  1. 32ν
  2. 2ν
  3. 3ν
  4. 23ν
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Since kmax = eVS = hν - φ
  2. eVS2 = hν - hν0     …(i)
  3. eVS = hν2 - hν0     …(ii)
  4. 12[hν2 - hν0] = hν - hν0
  5. ⇒ hν0 - hν02 = hν - hν4
  6. ⇒ hν02 = 3hν4
  7. ν0 = 3ν2
  8. * Language of question is wrongly framed. The values of stopping potentials should be interchanged.

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. For frequency ν: eVs2 = hν - hν0, so eVs = 2hν - 2hν0.
  2. For frequency ν2: eVs = hν2 - hν0.
  3. Equate: 2hν - 2hν0 = hν2 - hν0.
  4. hν0 = 2hν - hν2 = 32hν, so ν0 = 32ν, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 mediumagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsWrite Einstein's equation for the first light: e(V_s/2) = h(ν − ν₀). → Write it for the second light: eV_s = h(ν/2 − ν₀). → Eliminate V_s (double the first equation and equate) and solve the linear relation for ν₀.
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 3, 4
Option 1 is the result of the correct elimination; option 3 is what you land on if you forget to double the first equation (i.e. drop the factor of 2 on V_s/2) and option 4 is the reciprocal-style slip from solving ν₀ = 2ν − ν/2 the wrong way round, while option 2 (2ν) is the only one no clean mis-step produces.
why it is trickyThree short steps of standard photoelectric algebra, but the deciding work is entirely in handling the two factors of 2 — one on the frequency and one on the stopping potential — and two of the distractors sit exactly where those factors get mishandled, so elimination by plausibility does nothing.
the catchThe stem deliberately pairs the higher frequency with the SMALLER stopping potential, which looks physically backwards and tempts candidates to 'fix' the assignment before solving; combined with the dropped-factor-of-two options, a correct method still reaches a wrong key.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
An ideal gas undergoes four different processes from the same initial state as shown in the figure below. Those processes are adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric. The curve which represents the adiabatic process among 1, 2, 3 and 4 is
  1. 4
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. 3
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. (dPdV)adiabatic = -γ P
  2. (dPdV)isothermal = -P
  3. (dPdV)adiabatic > (dPdV)isothermal

→ the working concludes: unclear

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Curve 1 is vertical (V constant), so it is isochoric.
  2. Curve 4 is horizontal (P constant), so it is isobaric.
  3. For the isothermal process PV = const, so dPdV = -PV.
  4. For the adiabatic process PVγ = const, so dPdV = -γPV.
  5. Since γ > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
  6. Curve 2 is steeper than curve 3, so curve 2 is adiabatic, which is option 3.

why this chapterThe answer depends on how the applied voltage divides between two p-n junctions depending on whether each is forward or reverse biased (symmetric arrangements give equal drops).
subtopic 1PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopic 2PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
why subtopic 1The answer depends on recognising that the two series diodes are both identically biased in circuits (a) and (c) but one forward- and one reverse-biased in circuit (b), so the drops are equal only when both share the same bias state.
why subtopic 2Circuit (b) joins a PN and an NP junction in series, so one is reverse-biased and takes almost the whole drop, and ruling (b) out depends on that reverse-bias behaviour.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In the given circuits (a), (b) and (c), the potential drop across the two p-n junctions are equal in
  1. Both circuits (a) and (c)
  2. Circuit (a) only
  3. Circuit (b) only
  4. Circuit (c) only
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Potential drops across the p-n junctions will be same if either both junctions are forward biased or both junction are reverse biased.
  2. In figure (a) and (c), both junctions are forward biased therefore both have same potential.
  3. In figure (b) first junction is forward biased and second junction is reverse biased, so both junctions have different potential difference.

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented P→ N in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give V1 = V2.
  2. In circuit (b) one junction is P→ N and the other N→ P, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; Vforward ≪ Vreverse, so the drops are unequal.
  3. In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented N→ P in series, so both have the same bias and V1 = V2.
  4. Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsNotice that (a) and (c) are the same circuit mirrored (both diodes pointing the same way round the loop), so they must stand or fall together — options (2) and (4) die immediately. → Trace the loop in (a)/(c): both junctions face the same way relative to the battery, so both are forward biased (or both reverse) and carry identical drops. → Trace (b): the two diodes are back-to-back, so one is reverse biased and takes almost the entire supply voltage while the other takes ~0.7 V — drops unequal.
confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 3
Only (1) and (3) survive, because the mirror symmetry of (a) and (c) makes 'one of them only' impossible; (3) is a genuine trap for the student who reads the back-to-back pair in (b) as the 'symmetric' arrangement and assumes symmetry means equal potential drop.
why it is trickyMedium: the symmetry argument kills two options on sight, so the question collapses to a single binary choice, but that choice needs the real physics — that identically oriented diodes share the drop equally while an opposed pair has one element reverse biased hogging nearly all of it — and the geometrically symmetric circuit (b) is exactly the wrong answer a careless candidate reaches for.
the catchThe visual symmetry of circuit (b) points the opposite way from the electrical answer; the candidate must trace bias direction around the loop rather than judge by appearance.

Given below are half cell reactions:
MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O
E°Mn2+/MnO4- = -1.510 V
12O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O
E°O2/H2O = +1.223 V
Will the permanganate ion, MnO4- liberate O2 from water in the presence of an acid?
  1. No, because E°cell = - 2.733 V
  2. Yes, because E°cell = + 0.287 V
  3. No, because E°cell = - 0.287 V
  4. Yes, because E°cell = + 2.733 V
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- ⟶ Mn2+ + 4H2O     ...(i)
  2. E°MnO4-/Mn2+ = - E°Mn2+/MnO4- = 1.51 V
  3. H2O ⟶ 12O2 + 2H+ + 2e-     ...(ii)
  4. E°O2/H2O = 1.223 V
  5. Using 2 × (i) + 5 × (ii), net cell reactions is
  6. 2MnO4- + 6H+ ⟶ 2Mn2+ + 52O2 + 3H2O
  7. E°cell = E°C - E°A = E°MnO4-/Mn2+ - E°O2/H2O = 1.51 - 1.223 = 0.287 V
  8. Since E°cell > 0, therefore net cell reaction is spontaneous and so MnO4- liberate O2 from H2O in presence of an acid.

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet

  2. Identify anode (oxidation) half-reaction: H2O → 12O2 + 2H+ + 2e-, which is the reverse of the given reduction 12O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O (E° = +1.223 V), so oxidation potential = -1.223 V.
  3. E°cell = E°reduction + E°oxidation = 1.510 + (-1.223) = +0.287 V.

    why this chapterThe answer turns on how human spermatogenesis differs from oogenesis (differentiation after meiosis, continuous meiosis from a stem cell population, initiation at puberty), which is gametogenesis in Human Reproduction.
    subtopic 1Male Gametogenesis (Spermatogenesis)
    subtopic 2Female Gametogenesis (Oogenesis)
    why subtopic 1The answer depends on the features that set spermatogenesis apart from oogenesis: differentiation after meiosis, continuous meiosis from a stem-cell population, and starting at puberty.
    why subtopic 2The stem asks which statements do not hold for oogenesis, so each statement must be checked against oogenesis (e.g. it begins before birth and also yields haploid gametes under LH and FSH) to exclude (a) and (d).
    printed in the booklet
    publisher’s solution, as printed
    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    Which of the following statements are true for spermatogenesis but do not hold true for Oogenesis?

    Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
    (a)It results in the formation of haploid gametes
    (b)Differentiation of gamete occurs after the completion of meiosis
    (c)Meiosis occurs continuously in a mitotically dividing stem cell population
    (d)It is controlled by the Luteinising hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) secreted by the anterior pituitary
    (e)It is initiated at puberty
    1. (b), (c) and (e) only
    2. (c) and (e) only
    3. (b) and (c) only
    4. (b), (d) and (e) only
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
    1. Option (1) is the correct answer.
    2. In both, spermatogenesis and oogenesis haploid gametes are formed. So (a) is true for both.
    3. The spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa (sperms) by the process called spermiogenesis. Hence, (b) is true for spermatogenesis only.
    4. Spermatogenesis and oogenesis both are controlled by LH and FSH secreted by the anterior pituitary. Hence (d) is true for both.
    5. Spermatogenesis is a continuous process that begins at puberty. So (e) is true for spermatogenesis. Oogenesis on the other hand begins during embryonic development of the female.

    → the working concludes: option 1

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
    1. (a) Both spermatogenesis and oogenesis form haploid gametes, so (a) is not exclusive to spermatogenesis.
    2. (b) Spermatids differentiate into sperms (spermiogenesis) after meiosis is complete; in oogenesis meiosis II finishes only after sperm entry, so (b) applies to spermatogenesis only.
    3. (c) Spermatogonia form a mitotically dividing stem-cell population that keeps entering meiosis; oogonia stop multiplying before birth, so (c) applies to spermatogenesis only.
    4. (d) Both processes are regulated by pituitary LH and FSH, so (d) is not exclusive.
    5. (e) Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, whereas oogenesis begins during foetal development, so (e) applies to spermatogenesis only.
    6. Hence (b), (c) and (e) only, which is option 1.
    printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
    11 highagree
    difficultyhard · 5 steps
    stepsCheck (a): haploid gametes result from both spermatogenesis and oogenesis — shared, so reject. → Check (b): in spermatogenesis spermiogenesis (differentiation) follows completed meiosis, whereas the oocyte grows/differentiates while still arrested in meiosis I and finishes meiosis II only after fertilisation — spermatogenesis only. → Check (c): spermatogonia remain a continuously mitotically dividing stem-cell pool feeding meiosis, while oogonia stop multiplying before birth — spermatogenesis only. → Check (d): both processes are driven by anterior-pituitary LH and FSH — shared, reject. → Check (e): spermatogenesis begins at puberty, oogenesis begins in foetal life — spermatogenesis only; combine (b), (c), (e).

    Options 1, 2 and 3 differ only in whether (b) and (e) are included: a candidate who thinks 'differentiation after meiosis' is generic to gametogenesis drops (b) and lands on 2, one who forgets that oogenesis actually starts in the foetus drops (e) and lands on 3, while only option 4 is clearly out because (d) names LH/FSH, which control both sexes.

    The recombination frequency between the genes a & c is 5%, b & c is 15%, b & d is 9%, a & b is 20%, c & d is 24% and a & d is 29%. What will be the sequence of these genes on a linear chromosome?

    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    Ten E.coli cells with 15N - dsDNA are incubated in medium containing 14N nucleotide. After 60 minutes, how many E.coli cells will have DNA totally free from 15N?
    1. 80 cells
    2. 20 cells
    3. 40 cells
    4. 60 cells
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
    1. From 10 parent E.coli cells
    2. 1st generation
    3. 2nd generation
    4. 3rd generation
    5. Therefore, after 60 minutes, 60 E.coli cells will have DNA totally free from 15N.

    → the working concludes: option 4

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
    1. E. coli divides once every 20 min, so in 60 min there are 6020 = 3 generations.
    2. Total cells after 3 generations: 10 × 23 = 80.
    3. Replication is semiconservative: the two original 15N strands of each parent DNA stay intact and end up in 2 cells, so cells carrying 15N = 10 × 2 = 20.
    4. Cells totally free of 15N = 80 - 20 = 60, which is option 4.
    printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
    44 highagree
    difficultyhard · 4 steps
    stepsRecall E. coli generation time = 20 min, so 60 min gives 3 rounds of replication → Compute total cells: 10 × 23 = 80 → Apply semi-conservative replication: the original 20 heavy (15N) strands are each conserved in a separate cell, so 20 cells still contain 15N → Subtract: 80 − 20 = cells with DNA totally free of 15N
    confusing options4 of 4 · options 1, 2, 3, 4
    80 is the total cell count (candidate who stops after the growth calculation), 20 is the number of cells that still carry a heavy strand (the complement, and the figure most often quoted in Meselson–Stahl drills), 40 is what you get if you wrongly count 2 heavy strands per original cell going into 2 hybrid cells each or assume only half the population replicated, and 60 is the correct remainder.
    why it is trickyHard: four linked steps (generation time → 2^n growth → conservation of the 20 parental heavy strands → subtraction), and every one of the four options is exactly the output of stopping at one of those steps, so elimination gives no help at all.
    the catchThe question joins two topics — bacterial growth kinetics (20-minute generation time, which the stem never supplies) and semi-conservative replication — and turns on the keyword 'totally free', which makes the answer the complement of the usual Meselson–Stahl figure rather than the figure itself.
